source.title: AlGhafa Evaluation Benchmark for Arabic Language Models
source.authors: Ebtesam Almazrouei; Ruxandra-Aimée Cojocaru; M. Baldo; Quentin Malartic; Hamza Alobeidli; Daniele Mazzotta; Guilherme Penedo; Giulia Campesan; Mugariya Farooq; Maitha Alhammadi; Julien Launay; Badreddine Noune

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream benchmark performance across different model sizes, bearing on V6, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws and uses Hoffmann et al. (2022) to guide its training-token choices; it does not test loss power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own downstream evaluations across model sizes bear on V6. Toxicity and fine-tuning results do not bear on the claim versions. Scaling-curve values in the figures are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces the AlGhafa benchmark and applies Hoffmann et al. (2022) to set training tokens for its 1B–14B models. It reports benchmark scores for those models. Figures 5 and 9 plot the size series on downstream tasks, but the text gives no values and makes no statement about how performance changes with scale. So no result can be read for V6. There are no loss measurements or fits for V1–V3 or V7, no fixed-size shape comparison for V4, and no loss scaling in other regimes for V5. The text's model comparisons (r5–r9) set models trained on different data against each other, not a scale series.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors present the AlGhafa benchmark, a 1B–14B Arabic model family trained to Hoffmann-optimal token counts (14B on about 258 GT, 4 epochs), a HandMade dataset and a toxicity analysis. On the aggregate benchmark their 14B model ranks second after Jais-13B. They draw no conclusion about scaling laws from their own results.
record.recipe_differences: The authors train models following Hoffmann et al.’s scaling-law guidance and describe token counts chosen to match its optimality prediction, but they do not fit loss curves or test predictions against measured losses.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream results vary by benchmark task: the text says Our-14B performs better on Belebele Ar-MSA, Belebele Ar-dialects and MCQ Exams Ar, while Jais-13B particularly excels on SOQAL Ar and XGLUE Ar.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the First Arabic Natural Language Processing Conference (ArabicNLP 2023)
record.problems: The text gives no numerical average scores for the model-size comparison in Figure 5 and no uncertainty estimates. The qualitative task comparisons do not establish downstream performance as a function of scale; training data and setup also vary across the compared public models.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant outcomes were omitted. Figure 3’s aggregate comparison with external Arabic models is not separately rowed because its values are only shown graphically and the text’s explicit model comparisons are recorded in r5–r9.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported or fitted.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
Hoffmann allocation is applied, not tested; no loss-minimising allocation measured.
No fixed-size depth or width comparison.
Repeated-epoch runs (Figure 8) report only downstream accuracy shown graphically, with no loss scaling.
Size-series downstream results (Figures 5, 9) are figure-only with no stated trend; no link to pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices analysed.

missing.what: Few-shot (0–8 shots) accuracy per task and on average for the 1B, 3B, 7B and 14B size series. Values are graphical only.
1B models trained on 45, 90 and 135 GT (1, 2 and 3 epochs of a 45 GT dataset), zero-shot accuracy. Graphical only.
Aggregate zero-shot average and score* for the size series alongside public models

record.verdict_notes: I removed the reader's limits_scope label on V6. Rows r5–r9 compare differently trained models, so they say nothing about scale, and the size-series rows cannot be read. If figure values were digitised, Figures 3, 5 and 9 could give a V6 test, at T3 (Arabic setting).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss measurements or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute fits.
No small-run loss fits or comparisons of their predictions with larger runs.
The authors use Hoffmann et al. to select training token counts, but do not measure loss-minimising allocations or estimate allocation exponents.
No controlled comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests across modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
The study evaluates Arabic downstream benchmarks across model sizes, but does not test the relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss or give numerical scaling fits.
No analysis of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Zero-shot AlGhafa task comparisons between Our-14B and Jais-13B
reader_labels.reason: The text reports different models excelling on different tasks—Our-14B on two Belebele tasks and MCQ Exams Ar, Jais-13B on SOQAL Ar and XGLUE Ar—so performance is task-dependent; these comparisons do not establish a numerical scale trend (r5–r9).
